newsitem.title: USA: US CFTC moves toward lifting ag trade option ban.
newsitem.headline: US CFTC moves toward lifting ag trade option ban.

text.p: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission took a step on Monday towards allowing country grain elevators and others to offer agricultural trade options in competition with the Chicago Board of Trade and other futures exchanges.

The CFTC said in a notice published in the Federal Register that it would address the issue and asked interested parties to respond to 30 questions on aspects of eliminating the ban, which has been in place since 1936.

Last month, the CFTC's division of economic analysis recommended that the commission consider lifting the ban, "subject to appropriate conditions." And in a speech last week, CFTC Commissioner Joseph Dial expressed hope that the CFTC would lift the ban by October.

Randy Gordon, vice-president of communications for the National Grain and Feed Association, said his group had hoped the CFTC would move much quicker to lift ban following last month's staff recommendation.

"It's not as far or as fast as we wish they would have gone," Gordon said, referring to the CFTC's request for more public comment in its Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, one of the slower approaches to introducing regulations.
Nonetheless, the group shares Dial's hope that a final rule can be in place by fall, he said.
Lifting the ban would allow country grain elevators to offer farmers new products for managing risk, such as options contracts that would allow farmers to lock in revenue levels.
Congress banned agricultural options trading -- both on and off exchanges -- in the 1936 Commodity Exchange Act.

The ban on agricultural options trading on futures exchanges was lifted in 1984, after Congress gave CFTC the authority to review the issue. But the agency kept the ban on off-exchange option trading because of concerns over abuse.

The CFTC proposed lifting the ban on off-exchange agricultural trade options in 1991. Disagreement over the issue in the agricultural community killed that effort, but support for ending the ban has grown since then, Dial said last week.

"It is my hope that the commission's final action on ag trade options will be completed by this coming October," Dial said. That would allow off-exchange trading in agricultural options to begin as early as the 1998 crop year, he said.
The CFTC will accept comments on the issue through July 24.
